title: The Days of Awe
hook: ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur for making amends

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esau runs: the wronged brother moving first. Your line was he ran to meet him. Did you take your one small step? Today, the end of the week, and a season built for everything we've heard in it. Day nine hundred forty-five.

Two dates circled on a kitchen calendar. Next to the first, someone has drawn a little ram's horn. Next to the second, a single word: fast. Between them, the squares are full of small notes. Call Mom. Coffee with Dan. Write to Mr. Levin. Return the drill. It looks like an ordinary to-do list. It isn't. It's a list of people. In the Jewish year, the stretch between those two circles has a name, and it's built for exactly what this week has been about: turning back, and going to the people you've wronged.
screen: `TWO DATES CIRCLED.` → `A LIST OF PEOPLE.` → `A SEASON FOR TURNING BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the calendar. Leviticus sets the two days. In the King James words: "In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation." That's the day Jews call Rosh Hashanah, the new year. And then: "Also on the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a day of atonement." Yom Kippur. From the first day to the tenth: ten days. In Hebrew they're called the Yamim Noraim, the Days of Awe. Second, the picture. Tradition says, in a teaching in the Talmud, that on the new year the books are opened, and on the Day of Atonement they're sealed. Those in between have until then. It's an image, and readers hold it in different ways, but it gives the days their feel: a door that's open, and won't stay open forever. Third, the work. A prayer in the liturgy for these days names three things that turn aside the harsh decree: repentance, prayer and charity. Teshuvah, which opened this week. Prayer. And giving. Fourth, this whole week in one season. Forgiveness. The turn back. Maimonides' four steps. Asking the person first. Joseph weeping. Esau running. Joseph and Esau are read at other times of the year, but the turning, the steps and the asking all come due in these ten days. That's what the season is for: the apology that's been waiting, the call you keep putting off, made inside a window with a closing date, before the second circle on the calendar.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY AND THE TENTH.` · `THE BOOKS OPEN, THEN CLOSE.` · `REPENTANCE, PRAYER, CHARITY.` · `THIS WEEK, IN ONE SEASON.` · then, large: `TEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. In your mind, open a blank page. Now let names come, one at a time, of people you owe something: an apology, a thank-you that's overdue, a call, a thing to return. Don't judge the list. Don't rank it. Just let each name arrive and write it down in your head. When no more come, look over the page once. Then pick a closing date for yourself, ten days from today. If you pray, you can hold the list in your prayer, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Yamim Noraim. The ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, set aside for teshuvah, prayer, charity, and making amends. Today's word.
Your line: ten days. Write the list down for real today, and cross off one name before tonight. Day nine hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: During the Days of Awe, Jews pray special prayers, hear the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, give charity, and seek out people they have wronged to ask forgiveness before Yom Kippur.

notes: Week-end day (939–945); the teach looks back over the week.
Ten days: Leviticus 23:24 and 23:27 give the first and tenth days of the seventh month; 'ten days' counts both ends, as the tradition does.
Rosh Hashanah 16b (books opened on Rosh Hashanah, sealed on Yom Kippur; those in between suspended until Yom Kippur) paraphrased under 'tradition says'. The number of books is deliberately not given.
Unetaneh Tokef: 'repentance, prayer and charity avert the severity of the decree' paraphrased; no PD translation used. No date or author is given for the prayer.
The hook's calendar names (Dan, Mr. Levin) are invented for the scene.
Original-language entry יָמִים נוֹרָאִים: confirm vocalization and pronunciation.
Editor pass: cut the closing uplift line 'a deadline, it turns out, can be a mercy' and ended the teach on the hook's calendar instead.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): 'every one of them fits inside these ten days' overstated (the Joseph and Esau readings fall at other times of year); reworded. Leviticus 23:24, 23:27 KJV checked exact; Rosh Hashanah 16b and Unetaneh Tokef paraphrases fair.
